title: Character Analysis
description: Full character analysis of Christopher, Ed, Judy, Siobhan, Mrs Shears, Mrs Alexander, Roger Shears,.
content_html:
Character in a Play: What to Analyse

Because you are studying a play, character analysis should focus on theatrical presentation: how does Stephens use dialogue, stage directions, the play-within-a-play structure, and the ensemble to construct each character? How do characters function in relation to the play's themes? Avoid treating characters as if they are real people — ask instead how Stephens uses them as dramatic tools.

Christopher Boone: The Centre of Everything

Christopher is fifteen years old, autistic, and mathematically gifted. He is onstage throughout the entire play — the action never moves beyond his direct experience. This staging choice reflects his role as the lens through which the audience sees everything: the graph-paper world of the play is his world. His literal interpretation of language, his need for routine and predictability, and his inability to tolerate certain sensory inputs are not presented as disabilities but as cognitive characteristics that produce both extraordinary capability (solving the murder, travelling alone to London) and genuine vulnerability.

Christopher's defining quality is his commitment to truth: 'I do not tell lies.' This is simultaneously his moral core and the source of his greatest suffering. He cannot reframe his father's deceptions as well-intentioned half-truths — a lie is a lie, regardless of motive. His truthfulness makes him more morally consistent than the neurotypical adults around him, most of whom lie for what they believe are good reasons.

Key Fact

Christopher's core principle is 'I do not tell lies.' His literal commitment to truth means he cannot reframe his father's lies as protective or well-intentioned — making Ed's deceptions uniquely destructive to their relationship.

Mathematics represents Christopher's relationship to certainty. He says: 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the patterns away.' And also: 'I think prime numbers are like life. They are very logical but you could never work out the rules, even if you spent all your time thinking about them.' The first quote shows his love of mathematical purity — things reduced to their irreducible truth. The second is an uncharacteristic acknowledgement of complexity: prime numbers, like life, resist total predictability. Both quotes are from Haddon's novel but appear in the play through Siobhan's narration, establishing Christopher's relationship to mathematics from early in the performance.

Ed Boone: Love and Deception

Ed is a boiler engineer — a practical man, good with his hands and systems, less equipped to manage emotional complexity. His love for Christopher is never in doubt: it is present in every scene, from his management of the police station to his confession in Act 2, from his remorse to the gift of Sandy. But his love is expressed through protection rather than honesty, and his idea of protection leads him to construct an elaborate architecture of lies.

Ed killed Wellington in a moment of rage and grief after his relationship with Mrs Shears collapsed. He told Christopher his mother was dead because he could not face explaining that she had chosen to leave. Each lie required further lies to sustain it. Stephens presents Ed as a man whose emotional intelligence is not equal to his love — he knows how to fix a boiler but not how to tell his son the truth about the world. His complexity is one of the play's most important features: he is neither hero nor villain but a damaged, loving parent who made catastrophically wrong choices.

Key Fact

Ed lies about killing Wellington and about Judy being dead. His love for Christopher is genuine, but his emotional intelligence does not match his emotional investment — he protects Christopher through deception rather than honesty. Stephens presents him as complex, not simply villainous.

Judy Boone: Absence and Guilt

Judy is absent for most of the play — she exists through her letters and through Christopher's discovery of them. When she does appear in Act 2, she is overwhelmed with guilt and love simultaneously. Her letter contains the line: 'I am not a very good mother, Christopher. Maybe if things had been different... maybe if you'd been different... but that is not your fault.' This is one of the play's most emotionally complex moments: Judy is honest about her failure, acknowledges the unspoken difficulty of parenting Christopher, but refuses to let him carry the blame.

Judy represents a different kind of honesty from Christopher's: a messy, imperfect honesty that acknowledges failure without excusing it. She did leave her son. She did have an affair with Roger Shears. She was not a good mother in the sense of being consistently present. But she loves Christopher, and her letters — however delayed their arrival — are evidence of that love's persistence.

Siobhan: Teacher, Narrator, Mirror

Siobhan is Christopher's teacher at his special school — a figure of clarity, calm, and consistent communication. She understands how to speak to Christopher precisely: 'Siobhan understands. When she tells me not to do something she tells me exactly what it is I am not allowed to do. I like this.' This is Christopher's definition of a trustworthy person: someone who communicates without ambiguity. Siobhan earns and maintains that trust throughout the play.

In the play-text, Siobhan's theatrical role is as co-narrator. She reads aloud from Christopher's book throughout the performance, giving voice to his written inner world while he enacts it physically. This dual function — teacher in the story, narrator of the story — is unique to Stephens's adaptation. In the novel, Siobhan encourages Christopher to write his book but does not narrate it. In the play, she gives his first-person voice theatrical presence. The play ends with Christopher asking her: 'Does that mean I can do anything Siobhan?' She is the one person whose answer will be truthful and therefore meaningful to him.

Siobhan is Christopher's teacher — a qualified educator at his special school — not a teaching assistant or support worker. The distinction matters in the exam: she holds the pedagogical authority that makes her a credible narrator and her final possible answer meaningful. When you write about Siobhan in the exam, describe her as 'Christopher's teacher' and analyse her co-narrator function in the play. This is the feature that distinguishes the Stephens play from Haddon's novel.

Mrs Shears, Mrs Alexander, and the Neighbourhood Web

Mrs Shears is Wellington's owner and Christopher's neighbour. Her relationship with Ed after Judy's departure complicates the family's story: Ed and Mrs Shears had some kind of relationship, which then fell apart — and it was the collapse of this relationship that led Ed to kill Wellington in anger. Mrs Shears therefore represents the chain of adult relationships and failures that surround Christopher without his knowledge.

Mrs Alexander is the elderly neighbour whose apparently casual disclosure — that Christopher's mother and Mr Shears had an affair — is one of the play's most significant plot turns. She is not malicious; she assumes Christopher already knows. Her role in the play is to be the unwitting catalyst for Christopher's investigation taking a personal turn. She demonstrates that the neighbourhood is a web of connected knowledge that Christopher has been deliberately kept outside.

Roger Shears, Reverend Peters, and Toby

Roger Shears (Mr Shears) is Mrs Shears's ex-husband, Judy's London partner, and the reason Ed's marriage collapsed. His hostility to Christopher's arrival in London provides the final pressure that sends Christopher back to Swindon. He represents the reality that the adult world outside Christopher's family is also complicated and unwelcoming.

Reverend Peters invigilates Christopher's A-level Mathematics exam — his presence provides institutional validation of Christopher's achievement. He is a minor but structurally important character whose role is to witness and certify what Christopher can do.

Toby is Christopher's pet rat — a constant companion whose simple needs Christopher can understand and meet. In a play full of human relationships whose complexity Christopher finds overwhelming, Toby represents a relationship Christopher can manage. His rescue from the Underground tracks is one of the play's most striking individual moments of courage.

Effective drama analysis requires attention to stagecraft — considering not just what happens but how the playwright shapes the audience's response through every element of performance and text. In your exam response, identify specific techniques and explain their effect precisely.

exam_tip_html: In character analysis questions, always connect character function to theatrical form. Siobhan's most important feature is her narrator role in the play-text — not just her personality. Ed's complexity is most usefully analysed through Stephens's dramatic structure (showing us his love in Act 1 before revealing his deceptions). Remember: you are analysing Stephens's theatrical choices, not describing what characters are like as people.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christopher's defining principle is 'I do not tell lies' — this makes Ed's deceptions uniquely devastating, because Christopher cannot reframe them as protective.
  • Siobhan is Christopher's teacher and the play's co-narrator — her dual role is unique to the Stephens play-text, not present in the novel.
  • Ed's moral complexity — genuine love expressed through devastating deception — is central to Stephens's exploration of the parent-child relationship.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present Christopher as a sympathetic and complex protagonist?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Christopher's complexity: logical commitment to truth making him morally consistent but vulnerable; his extraordinary capability (journey to London, A-level Maths) alongside genuine difficulty with social interaction; how Siobhan's narration generates audience sympathy by explaining his reasoning. AO4: neurodiversity context.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range and evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points about Christopher.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use Siobhan to guide the audience's understanding of Christopher?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Siobhan's dual function: teacher in the story and co-narrator of the play. Discusses how her narration gives the audience access to Christopher's reasoning that his dialogue cannot provide, the play-within-a-play structure as a theatrical solution to first-person narration, and her role in the final scene. AO2: theatrical device of co-narration.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with theatrical awareness.
Mid band (15-21): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic discussion.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens present the character of Ed Boone?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Ed's moral complexity. Discusses: genuine love (police station, Sandy), the interconnected deceptions, his confession and remorse, the idea that his emotional intelligence does not match his love. Explores the dramatic irony of Act 1 (audience will discover his lies) and range to the reconciliation. AO4: the challenge of single parenting a child with additional needs.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with range.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Stephens presents Judy as a character defined by absence and guilt.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Judy's construction through absence: present through letters before she appears, absent from Christopher's life physically. Discusses the letter ('I am not a very good mother... that is not your fault'), the reunion in Act 2, the contrast between emotional love and physical abandonment. AO2: how characters can be constructed through absence.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with evidence.
Mid band (15-21): Explained response.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Some points.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use the character of Mrs Alexander to explore the theme of hidden knowledge?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of Mrs Alexander's role as inadvertent catalyst. Discusses: her assumption that Christopher already knows about the affair, the dramatic irony of her disclosure, and what she represents (the adult world's shared knowledge that Christopher has been excluded from). Connects to wider theme of truth being concealed by those who love Christopher.
Mid-high band (22-28): Clear analysis with some range.
Mid band (15-21): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (8-14): Basic discussion.
Lower band (1-7): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Stephens use minor characters — Mrs Alexander, Reverend Peters, and Toby — to develop the play's themes?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (29-35): Perceptive analysis of how minor characters serve thematic functions. Mrs Alexander: hidden knowledge and the inadvertent revealer. Reverend Peters: institutional validation of Christopher's achievement. Toby: Christopher's capacity for care and reliable relationship in an unreliable world. Each serves a distinct thematic purpose beyond their plot function.

knowledge_checks.q: What is Christopher's core principle about truth?
options: Truth is complicated and sometimes harmful
'I do not tell lies' — an absolute, literal commitment to honesty
White lies are acceptable to protect people

knowledge_checks.q: What is Siobhan's role in the Stephens play that is NOT present in Haddon's novel?
options: Christopher's teacher at his special school
Co-narrator who reads aloud from Christopher's book throughout the performance
The person who encourages Christopher to write his book
The most trusted adult in Christopher's life

knowledge_checks.q: Christopher says: 'Prime numbers are what is left when you have taken all the _____ away.'
Judy's letter contains the line: 'I am not a very good mother... but that is not _____ fault.'
Match each character to their primary function in the play:
right: Teacher and co-narrator whose narration gives Christopher's inner world theatrical presence
Elderly neighbour who inadvertently reveals the affair between Judy and Roger Shears
School vicar who invigilates Christopher's A-level exam, providing institutional validation

flashcard_questions.q: What is Christopher's core principle about truth?
flashcard_questions.a: 'I do not tell lies' — an absolute, literal commitment to honesty that makes Ed's deceptions uniquely devastating.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Siobhan's job in the play?
flashcard_questions.a: Christopher's teacher at his special school — not a teaching assistant. She is also the play's co-narrator, reading from his book throughout the performance.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Siobhan's co-narrator role unique to the Stephens play?
flashcard_questions.a: In Haddon's novel, Christopher narrates in first person. Stephens gives that first-person voice to Siobhan, who reads it aloud — creating a play-within-a-play that is not present in the novel.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Christopher say he likes about how Siobhan communicates?
flashcard_questions.a: 'Siobhan understands. When she tells me not to do something she tells me exactly what it is I am not allowed to do. I like this.' Clear, precise, unambiguous communication.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Judy's letter reveal about her as a parent?
flashcard_questions.a: She is honest about her failure: 'I am not a very good mother.' She acknowledges the difficulty of Christopher's needs without blaming him: 'that is not your fault.'

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Ed described as morally complex rather than simply villainous?
flashcard_questions.a: His love for Christopher is genuine and consistent, but his emotional intelligence does not match his love — he protects Christopher through deception rather than honesty.

flashcard_questions.q: What role does Mrs Alexander play in the plot?
flashcard_questions.a: She tells Christopher about the affair between his mother and Mr Shears — an inadvertent disclosure that assumes Christopher already knew, triggering the chain of revelations in Act 2.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Toby the rat represent?
flashcard_questions.a: A relationship Christopher can manage: simple, dependable, loyal. In a world of confusing human relationships, Toby gives Christopher a form of care and responsibility he can reliably meet.

glossary_terms.definition: A second narrative voice — in the play, Siobhan reads Christopher's book aloud while he acts out events, sharing the narration with his physical performance.
The quality of a character who cannot be simply categorised as good or bad — Ed Boone is morally complex because his genuine love coexists with devastating deception.
The role a character plays in the overall structure and themes of the play — each character in The Curious Incident serves specific dramatic functions beyond their literal role.
A character who contrasts with another to highlight particular qualities — Siobhan's honesty and precision contrast with Ed's protective deception.
The central character whose journey drives the play's action — Christopher is the protagonist; the play tracks his investigation, journey, and growing understanding.
The playwright's use of dramatic techniques including staging, lighting, dialogue, and structure to create meaning.
The sense of anticipation or unease created by conflict, uncertainty, or approaching crisis in drama.
A recurring image, symbol, or idea in a text that carries thematic significance.
